Week 8 · Lessons 1 to 4 · The Gold Rush
What was life really like on the goldfields, and for whom?

Learning intention

To use texts, pictures and maps to find out what daily life was like on the goldfields for miners, women, children and Chinese diggers, and to write from their point of view.

Success criteria

  • I can find facts in a text and use them as evidence.
  • I can explain how people adapted to hard conditions.
  • I can write in the voice of a person from the 1850s.
  • I can say how the same events looked different to different people.
  • I can read an old map and match it to today.

Pick at least three. Any order. Tick them off as you finish.

Reading text · 1 of 6

Immigration boom

Reading level:Text adapted from Britannica Kids, "Australian gold rushes"

The gold rushes had an immense impact on Australia's population. News of the 1851 discoveries attracted people from countries around the world. Over just two decades, immigration quadrupled Australia's population, from 438,000 in 1851 to 1.7 million in 1871. As the population expanded, it also began to diversify. Other than the Aboriginal peoples, the colonial population before the gold rushes consisted almost entirely of people from the British Isles. Although the majority of the new immigrants also came from the United Kingdom, they were joined by prospectors from the United States, Germany, France, Italy, Poland, Hungary and other countries. The gold rush era was also the first time that Australia experienced a significant influx of Chinese immigrants. By 1861 more than 38,000 Chinese lived in Australia, making up more than 3 per cent of the population. More than 12,000 Chinese arrived in the year 1856 alone.

Gold was found in 1851. This brought people from many countries. Australia's population grew from 438,000 in 1851 to 1.7 million in 1871. Most still came from Britain, but others came from the United States, Germany, France, Italy, Poland and Hungary. Many came from China. By 1861 there were about 38,000 Chinese people in Australia. Over 12,000 arrived in 1856 alone.

Chinese prospectors experienced much hardship and mistreatment on the Australian goldfields. Most were under contract to Chinese and foreign businessmen. In exchange for their passage to Australia, they had to work until they paid off their debt and could then return to China. European and American diggers were suspicious of the Chinese, with their different language, clothes, food, religious practices and customs. Moreover, they resented the success of the Chinese and their unique mining methods. The Chinese were particularly hardworking and efficient. Unlike European and American miners, who worked alone or in small groups, the Chinese worked together in teams of 30 to 100 men. They preferred to rework claims that had been abandoned by other miners rather than exploring new ground. In this way, they often found gold that others had overlooked.

Chinese miners often worked in large teams of 30 to 100 and searched ground left by others, sometimes finding more gold. Many had borrowed money for the journey and had to work until it was paid back. Some Europeans did not like their language, food or customs, and were jealous of their success.

Strong anti-Chinese feeling arose on the goldfields, and many racially fuelled riots erupted. Some of the most violent took place at Lambing Flat (now Young) in New South Wales in 1860 and 1861. In the last of these, on 30 June 1861, some 3,000 European and American miners attacked a Chinese camp. They beat the Chinese, burned their tents and cut off their queues. In response, the New South Wales government passed the Chinese Immigration Act to greatly reduce the number of Chinese migrating to the colony. Restrictions were also introduced in Victoria (1855), South Australia (1857), Queensland (1877) and Western Australia (1886).

The Chinese faced unfair treatment. At Lambing Flat in 1860 to 1861, thousands of miners attacked Chinese camps and burned their tents. After this, the colonies made laws to limit Chinese immigration.

Reading text · 2 of 6

Life on the goldfields: getting there, and shelter

Reading level:Text adapted from Britannica Kids, "Australian gold rushes"

Living conditions on the goldfields were harsh for everyone: diggers, women and children. To reach the goldfields, prospectors usually had to travel long distances on foot, carrying all their possessions, because no roads had been built and horse transport was too expensive.

Reaching the goldfields was hard. Most people walked, carrying their belongings, because there were no roads and horses cost too much.

Once they arrived, they had to set up tents for shelter. Early tents were very simple, usually a piece of canvas draped over a tree branch. They were not secure, and on many occasions miners had their belongings stolen. The tents also gave little protection from snakes and insects. These conditions are one reason why men usually travelled to the goldfields alone in the early years of a rush. Their families would join them later, once diggers had made their dwellings more livable.

At first they lived in tents, which were unsafe and gave little protection from snakes or insects. Things got stolen. So men often came alone at first, and families came later.

If a miner was able to establish a profitable claim, he would typically build a bark hut. Some diggers who decided to stay for a long time, or who had brought their families, built more permanent homes. They constructed huts using wooden slabs, mud bricks, or wattle and daub. These homes were small and cramped, with only one or two rooms for the whole family. The children usually slept together in one bed and the parents in another. A fireplace was used for cooking and for heat in winter. Furniture was sparse and handmade from wood and any other materials on hand, such as recycled boxes. Only wealthy miners could afford more elaborate furnishings. On the more populated and profitable goldfields, houses, hotels and shops were established.

If a miner found gold, he might build a bark hut. Families later built huts from wood slabs, mud bricks, or wattle and daub. These homes were small and cramped, with one or two rooms and a fireplace for heat and cooking. Furniture was simple and homemade. Only rich miners had better houses.

Reading text · 3 of 6

Food and water

Reading level:Text adapted from Britannica Kids, "Australian gold rushes"

Many people became disillusioned with life on the goldfields. Most foods were in short supply and therefore very expensive. The typical digger's diet was restricted and repetitive, consisting mostly of meat and damper. Meat was readily available from local pastoralists with herds of sheep and cattle. The staple meat, especially in the early days, was mutton (sheep). Because there was no refrigeration, meat had to be eaten within a short time. Sometimes meat was preserved by rubbing salt over it. Bacon, ham, butter and cheese were luxury items that only successful miners could afford.

Food was scarce and expensive. Most miners ate mutton (sheep meat) and damper (a simple bread). Without refrigeration, meat spoiled quickly. Sometimes it was preserved with salt. Luxuries like butter, bacon or cheese were rare.

Clean drinking water was hard to find. Rivers and creeks were polluted by the mining process and, in the absence of a sanitation system, by human waste. Water had to be boiled to make it safe to drink. Diggers drank black tea with most meals. They prepared it by boiling water over a campfire in a tin pot called a billy. They drank it from a tin mug called a pannikin.

Clean water was hard to find. Rivers were polluted by mining and human waste. Water had to be boiled before drinking. Miners drank black tea from a tin billy and pannikin.

In the early gold rush years, miners were not permitted to plant vegetable gardens. This policy was meant to discourage miners from establishing permanent homes. In 1853, however, the Victorian government allowed vegetable gardens on the goldfields. Chinese immigrants played a vital role in supplying fresh vegetables, and the diggers came to rely on this produce. Most of the Chinese prospectors had come from southern China, where they had worked as farmers. As the gold supply declined, many Chinese turned to market gardening. They settled near towns and cities and became successful business owners. Many profited more from providing fresh food than from searching for dwindling gold.

In 1853, miners were allowed to grow vegetables. Chinese gardeners supplied much of this food, which was important for health. Later many became successful business owners.

Reading text · 4 of 6

Health, disease and danger

Reading level:Text adapted from Britannica Kids, "Australian gold rushes"

The poor living conditions made it difficult to stay healthy. Infectious diseases spread easily through the settlements. Many people became ill with typhoid fever, cholera or dysentery, all caused by contaminated water or food. Diets lacking fresh fruit and vegetables led to scurvy. Other common diseases included influenza, pneumonia, scarlet fever and diphtheria. Medical treatment was hard to find and too expensive for most miners. Those who could not afford a doctor often turned to apothecaries, who made medicines from plants and other local ingredients, gave medical advice, performed surgery and delivered babies.

Conditions on the goldfields made people sick. Typhoid, cholera and dysentery spread in dirty water. A lack of fruit and vegetables caused scurvy. Doctors were expensive. Many miners went to apothecaries, who made medicines from plants, gave advice and sometimes did surgery.

Mining was a dangerous pursuit, and accidents were common. Diggers were trapped by collapsing mine shafts and injured by machinery. They were also exposed to poisonous gases in mine tunnels. Many mining accidents were deadly. In the town of Ballarat alone, one miner was killed in an accident on average every week in 1859.

Mining was dangerous. Miners were hurt by collapsing shafts, machinery and poisonous gases. In Ballarat in 1859, one miner was killed every week in an accident.

!Learn this

Why does this matter for your writing? Every one of these dangers is a feeling for a letter writer: fear for a child in winter, worry when a husband is late home from the shaft.

Reading text · 5 of 6

Women

Reading level:Text adapted from Britannica Kids, "Australian gold rushes"

Men were always a majority on the goldfields, but the number of women grew as the years went on. Ballarat, for example, had 4,023 women living alongside 12,660 men in 1854. By 1861 the proportion of women had increased significantly, with 9,135 women compared to 12,726 men. Most were wives who joined their husbands a few years after a rush began, but a small number were single. Women played an important role in many ways. A few dug for gold, with their husbands or on their own. Some made clothes, hats or shoes. Others set up shops or ran hotels. Most women, however, worked in the home, doing domestic duties and raising children. Some chores, such as cooking and washing dishes, were done every day. Others were scheduled for certain days. The most difficult day was washing day. After miners spent all day digging in mud or clay, their clothes were filthy. Everything had to be washed by hand, soaked in soapy water and scrubbed on a washboard. Other days were set aside for cleaning, sewing and mending, baking, and ironing with an iron heated over the fire. All bread, jams, soap and candles had to be made by hand. If a family owned a cow, the women milked it and made butter.

At first, most people on the goldfields were men. But by 1861, many women had joined them. In Ballarat there were over 9,000 women living with about 12,000 men. Women did many different jobs. Some dug for gold. Some ran shops, hotels or small businesses. Others made and sold clothes, hats and shoes. Most women worked at home: cooking, cleaning, washing clothes and looking after children. Washing was the hardest job, all by hand on a washboard. Monday was often wash day. Other days were for sewing, baking, ironing or making butter. Women also made their own bread, jam, soap and candles. Their work was essential to a family's survival.

!Learn this

To meet a real woman of the goldfields, ask your teacher for the Eliza Perrin story from the Gold Museum, Ballarat.

Reading text · 6 of 6

Children

Reading level:Text adapted from Britannica Kids, "Australian gold rushes"

Life could be both difficult and exciting for children. They were expected to help with many household chores: fetching water from the well or river, gathering firewood, feeding the horses, washing clothes and looking after younger siblings. Older children often helped on the diggings. They shovelled rock and gravel, panned for gold and worked the rocker. Children were not required to go to school. Parents who chose to send them had to pay, and some could not afford it. Some parents kept children home to help with chores and prospecting, and some sent sons to school but not daughters, thinking girls could learn what they needed (knitting, sewing, cooking, cleaning, ironing) at home. The first classes were held in tents the teacher could take down and move. Later, religious groups held classes in churches, and eventually the government built schools in the larger settlements.

Children worked hard. They fetched water, gathered firewood, fed animals, washed clothes and cared for younger brothers and sisters. Older children sometimes helped with panning for gold. School was not free or required. Some parents sent their sons, but many girls stayed home to learn housework. Schools were first held in tents or churches, later in government buildings.

When not helping at home or at school, children amused themselves with whatever was around. They played marbles, jacks and quoits (throwing rope rings over a peg). They played jacks using knucklebones. Other toys included wooden soldiers, rag dolls, skipping ropes, blocks and spinning tops. Children, with the rest of the family, took a bath once a week: water heated in a kettle and poured into a tin tub, one person at a time. Children were at the greatest risk from infectious diseases. Although a smallpox vaccine existed, there were no vaccines for other diseases. With poor nutrition, sanitation and medical supplies, many babies and young children died.

In their spare time, children played with marbles, rag dolls, spinning tops, wooden blocks or knucklebones. Bathing was once a week in a tin tub, one person at a time. Children were at high risk from diseases. Many babies and young children died from poor food, illness and lack of medicine.

Activity 4 · Newspaper report 50 min plus Canva

Activity 4: The immigration boom

You are a newspaper reporter in the 1850s. Write a three or four paragraph article about the immigration boom on the goldfields.
Choose your reporter

Sympathetic reporter: celebrates the new arrivals and what they bring.

Critical reporter: shows the suspicion and resentment many European diggers felt.

Read this first

Historians read hostile old newspapers as evidence of what people thought at the time. If you choose the critical reporter you are showing what some people believed in 1861, not what you believe. Use the facts in the text; do not invent insults. At the end you will step out of the role and say what your article tells a historian.

✎In your book

Heading: Activity 4: Newspaper report. Write which reporter you are. Then the evidence grid (next card), the plan, and the article.

Part 3 of 6
Activity 4 · Step 2 · Mentor text

How a report is built

Masthead The newspaper's name, the place and the price. Ballarat Times, 10c.
Headline Big, short, punchy. Three words that pull you in: Mud, Mutton and Misery.
Subheading One line that says what the story is about.
Byline Who wrote it, where and when: Special Correspondent, Ballarat, 1859.
Lead paragraph The most important idea first: life is harsher than expected.
Facts Every paragraph has evidence: mutton and damper, boiled water, one death a week.
Closing line A sentence that sums up the reporter's view.
Picture with caption A real image, credited.
Part 4 of 6
Activity 4 · Step 3 · Plan, then write

Plan the four paragraphs

Paragraph planner (or make your own)
  1. Introduction. The boom: huge population growth, arrivals from China and many other countries.
  2. Facts and details. The numbers, where people came from, how Chinese miners worked in teams.
  3. Contributions. Reworking abandoned claims, market gardens feeding the goldfields.
  4. Challenges and conflict. Suspicion and resentment, Lambing Flat. End with your reporter's view: hopeful, or hostile.
Reporter's voice: starters

Sympathetic: The goldfields are thriving thanks to hardworking Chinese miners who rework abandoned claims with great success.

Critical: European diggers are increasingly angered by the flood of Chinese arrivals, whose different ways set them apart.

Headline and byline

Sympathetic: Chinese Miners Boost Goldfields with Skill and Dedication

Critical: Thousands of Chinese Crowd the Fields, Stirring Tensions

Byline: your name, then special correspondent or on the scene reporter, the place, the year.

✎In your book

Headline, byline, then the article. Three or four paragraphs. Underline every fact you took from the grid.

Now be yourself again

!Learn this

Newspapers change what people think. In 1861 some reporters wrote fairly about Chinese miners and some wrote unfairly, and the unfair ones helped cause Lambing Flat. Your article shows a historian what people believed then. It does not show what you believe.

Swap with a partner
  1. Read each other's articles. Find one fact you both used.
  2. Did you use the same fact to make readers feel different things? How?
✎In your book

Last line, in your own voice, not the reporter's: My article shows that in 1861 some people believed ...

TeacherKeep this to five minutes. The pair swap is the point: same fact, opposite feeling. Read two headlines aloud side by side if there is time.

Activity 5 · Letter home 45 min

Activity 5: A letter home from the goldfields

Write a letter to someone back home, as a person living on the goldfields. In Week 9 you will turn it into a monologue and perform it. If you already have a Digger's Log character, be that person.

Facts you can use

  • By 1861 Ballarat had 9,135 women and 12,726 men.
  • Some women dug for gold, some ran shops, hotels or made clothes; most ran the home.
  • Washing day was the hardest: soaking, scrubbing on a washboard, all by hand.
  • Bread, jam, soap and candles all made at home.
  • Eliza Perrin ran a refreshment house at Ballarat to earn money when her husband could not.

Facts you can use

  • Children fetched water, gathered firewood, fed horses, minded younger siblings.
  • Older children shovelled gravel, panned and worked the rocker.
  • School cost money and was not compulsory. Some families sent sons but not daughters.
  • Games: marbles, knucklebones, quoits, spinning tops.
  • Bath once a week in a tin tub; children caught diseases most easily.

Facts you can use

  • More than 12,000 Chinese arrived in 1856 alone; most came from farming villages in southern China.
  • Many owed money for their passage and had to work until it was paid, then return home.
  • Worked in teams of 30 to 100, reworking claims others had given up.
  • Faced suspicion for language, clothes, food and customs; at Lambing Flat, tents were burned and queues cut off.
  • Many later became market gardeners and business owners.
✎In your book

Heading: Activity 5: Letter home. Write who you are (name, age, job) and who you are writing to.

TeacherMary Anne Allen is named in the original pack as a mother who wrote about the dangers of goldfields family life; no text of hers is in the pack, so she is used only for tone here. Verify the Eliza Perrin Gold Museum Ballarat post before sharing the link.
Part 2 of 3
Activity 5 · Three paragraphs

Plan, then write

1 · Your day

What chores, jobs or routines fill your day? Start with a real detail: Yesterday I washed clothes for hours ...

2 · The conditions

What is the food like? What dangers or illnesses are around you? Use two facts from your fact bank.

3 · Your feelings

What worries you most? What do you hope for? I pray the children stay healthy this winter ...

!Learn this

Voice. Write as if you are speaking to the person. Facts and feelings together: one fact, then what it does to you. Small details make it real: the smell of the tent, the price of flour, the sound of the cradle.

✎In your book

Date at the top (a real year, 1852 to 1861), Dear ..., three paragraphs, a sign-off. Underline your facts.

A little extra helpOne paragraph for each box, three sentences each, using the starters.
CoreThree full paragraphs, at least four facts.
ExtensionWrite the reply from home, or add a postscript written a year later.
Part 3 of 3
Activity 5 · Next week

From letter to monologue

A monologue is one person speaking aloud to an audience. Your letter becomes the script.

Turning it into speech
  1. Cross out Dear and the sign-off. Start in the middle of a thought.
  2. Choose one line to say straight to the audience, as if they are your family.
  3. Mark two places to pause. Mark one place to speed up.
  4. Pick one object to hold: a tin mug, a piece of cloth, a stone.
!Learn this

Real monologues are short. Sixty seconds of speaking is about 130 words. Cut anything that does not carry a fact or a feeling.

✎In your book

On your letter, mark the cuts and pauses in a different colour. Practise it once quietly.

TeacherThis feeds the Week 9 perspectives lessons and the Digger's Log diary; a girl who writes as her Log character has her monologue script done.

Activity 6: Melbourne grows

Four old maps and one river. Follow the Yarra from before the gold rush to today and watch a city appear around it.

✎In your book

Heading: Activity 6: Melbourne grows. Get the printed map pack. On each map, trace the Yarra in blue and label the year. Stick them in order down the page.

▶On screen

Scroll down. The maps are in date order, biggest first. Click any map to zoom right in; the magnifier is on by default.

1835Melbourne founded on Wurundjeri land.
1843 and 1848Surveyors' maps of paddocks by the river.
1851Gold. Melbourne is 16 years old.

Part 2 of 6
Activity 6 · Before the gold

Before the gold: 1843 and 1848

These are surveyors' sketches of Richmond, a few minutes' walk east of the city grid. The wiggly line is the Yarra. The squares are blocks of land with the names of the people who bought them. Everything else is blank because nothing was there.

Look for
  • The bend of the Yarra. You will find this same bend on every map, including today's.
  • How much of the sheet is empty.
✎In your book

Under your 1843 and 1848 maps: Before gold, this land was ... (one sentence).

Part 3 of 6
Activity 6 · After the gold

After the gold: 1857

Six years after gold. Bradshaw's map was sold to railway passengers. Zoom in: the Yarra, Hobsons Bay, the neat grid of the city, railways, churches, suburbs in every direction.

Find on the map
  • The Yarra and where it meets the sea at Hobsons Bay.
  • The Hoddle Grid: the neat rectangle of streets north of the river.
  • Emerald Hill, south of the river. In 1852 this was Canvas Town, thousands of tents for new arrivals.
  • Railway lines. Australia's first steam railway opened here in 1854.
  • The Richmond bend from the 1843 map. What is drawn around it now?
✎In your book

Under your 1857 map: three things that are new since 1848.

Part 4 of 6
Activity 6 · After the gold

After the gold: 1859

Two years later, a government map of what the land is made of. The city grid is top left. The colours are rock and soil types. Look how far the streets now reach.

Find on the map
  • Two cricket grounds east of the city. One is the MCG.
  • Jolimont, where Governor La Trobe's cottage stood.
  • Streets that were not on the 1857 map.
✎In your book

Under your 1859 map: By 1859 Melbourne had ...

Part 5 of 6
Activity 6 · Today

Today

Same river, same grid. Drag and zoom. Switch to Satellite to see the real thing.

Scroll to zoom, drag to move.
Find on both the 1857 map and today's
  • The Hoddle Grid: still the middle of the city.
  • Flinders Street along the river (the station opened in 1854).
  • The MCG in the paddock east of the city.
  • Emerald Hill, now called South Melbourne.
  • Sandridge on the bay, now Port Melbourne, where the ships landed.
  • The Richmond bend from 1843. What is on those paddocks now?
